plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a one-dimensional imaging system in flatland, a simplified 2D world used to build intuition for camera modeling. The scene is represented as a line of varying light intensities at a fixed depth, and the sensor axis is reversed relative to the scene, consistent with pinhole geometry. The figure sets up the linear algebra framework for treating cameras as linear systems, where the camera maps a world intensity vector to a sensor measurement vector.

interactionPlan.concept: A pinhole camera maps positions in a 1D scene to a 1D sensor using straight-line ray projection, which naturally inverts the spatial coordinates of the image.
elements: Top number line axis for scene, labeled 0 to 12 from left to right with axis label 'n'
1D array of 13 square boxes representing the scene, labeled 'l_w' on left and 'Scene' on right
Highlighted active pixel in the scene array (red)
Thick black horizontal line representing the occluder, labeled 'Occluder' on left and 'Aperture' on right
A small gap in the occluder representing the pinhole, with a 'Pinhole' text and arrow pointing to it
Bundle of red arrows (light rays) originating from the center of the active scene pixel, spreading downwards
A single red arrow from the bundle passing perfectly through the pinhole and hitting the sensor
Bottom 1D array of 13 square boxes representing the sensor, labeled 'l_s' on left and 'Camera sensor' on right
Highlighted active pixel in the sensor array (red) where the ray lands
Bottom number line axis for the sensor, labeled with tick marks and 'n'

interactions.label: Light source position (n)
interactions.teaches: Moving the source point shifts the angle of the emitted rays; only the specific ray aligned with the pinhole dictates which sensor pixel lights up.

interactions.label: Sensor axis direction
interactions.teaches: Because the pinhole physically inverts the image (left becomes right), reversing the sensor's indexing coordinates mathematically compensates for this flip, aligning sensor indices with scene indices.

demo_steps.title: Pinhole projection
demo_steps.narration: A point in the scene scatters light in all directions, but the occluder blocks all but one ray. This creates a one-to-one mapping between scene points and sensor pixels.

demo_steps.title: Spatial inversion
demo_steps.narration: Try sliding the light source to position 10. Notice that moving the source rightwards causes the projected point on the sensor to move leftwards—the geometry naturally inverts the image.

demo_steps.title: Compensating with coordinates
demo_steps.narration: To make the math linear and intuitive (so scene pixel 'n' maps to sensor pixel 'n'), we define the sensor's coordinate system in reverse, counteracting the physical flip.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The pinhole creates a one-to-one mapping that physically inverts the incoming light; reversing the sensor's coordinate axis is a mathematical convenience to un-flip the data.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Align the scene array, the pinhole, and the sensor array so they share a central vertical axis (position 6). Ensure the ray passing through the pinhole originates at scene pixel index `x` and physically lands on the sensor at distance `12-x` from the left. Draw 5-7 red rays total from the active scene pixel, with only the one passing through the pinhole extending all the way to the sensor; the others should terminate exactly at the black occluder line. When the 'sensorAxis' toggle is flipped, visually reverse the numbers on the bottom axis (0 on left to 12 on right, instead of 12 on left to 0 on right).

authoredContext:
A one dimensional imaging system in flatland. As in , we have reversed the direction of the sensor coordinates.

Let the light intensities in the world be represented by a column vector, $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$. The value of the $n$-th component of $\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{w}}$ gives the intensity of the light at position $n$, heading in the direction of the camera. There are a few more things to notice in -flatland_camera_linear. The first one is that the axis in the camera sensor is reversed, consistent with -pinholeGeometry. The value $n$ corresponds to image coordinates and the units are pixels. The second is that we are modeling the scene as being a line with varying albedos at a fixed depth from the camera. If the scene had a more complex spatial structure we would have to use the light field in order to use the same linear algebra that we will use in this chapter to model cameras. We will use light fields in -nerfs.

discrepancies: The label 'Camera sensor' is clipped at the right edge of the figure canvas.
The 'w' and 's' in ℓ_w and ℓ_s are positioned as standalone text elements rather than proper subscripts, making them look slightly disconnected from the ℓ symbol.

The scattered rays in the generated figure fan out symmetrically, whereas in the source figure they predominantly hit the left side of the occluder, reflecting the left-biased position of the active light source.
evaluation.notes: The generated interactive figure correctly implements the geometry and physics of a pinhole camera, adding a highly pedagogical slider to demonstrate the projection inversion, though a minor layout oversight causes one label to clip.
action_items: Move the 'Camera sensor' label slightly to the left (e.g., change its center to `cx(690)`) so it does not clip against the right edge of the 800px viewbox.
Adjust the relative positioning of the 'w' and 's' text elements (or use a tspan) to format them as proper, tightly-kerned subscripts of the 'ℓ' symbol.
